Vignette:
Three years prior, the pavement of Elias Vance’s district had simply ceased to belong to him. He was twenty-two, working as a civilian logistics coordinator when the front lines fractured outward, swallowing the residential blocks he navigated daily for supply drops. The violence did not announce itself with warnings; it arrived as sudden, concussive impacts that turned courtyards into rubble and turned neighbors into silhouettes against smoke. Elias remembered the precise geometry of the basement stairwell where he crouched for three days, the taste of concrete dust in his mouth, and the way the ground jumped beneath him every time an explosion rolled over the ridge. What frightened him most was not the noise itself, but the sudden, inescapable certainty that survival was a matter of sheer, arbitrary luck. He walked away with his body intact, but the quiet aftermath left him carrying a heavy, unshakable reservoir of fear and horror. Alongside it settled a sharp, persistent guilt over the colleagues who never left the building, and a quiet, gnawing shame for the fact that he was the one who had made it out. When he returned home, the architecture of his days shifted without his permission. During daylight, he could move through his routines, though the emotional weight never lifted. What frightened him most, however, was what happened after dusk. He found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day. The familiar hum of his apartment complex transformed into something dense and charged. He began pacing the hallway until his knees ached, checking the deadbolt three times, then five, convinced that stillness was a luxury he could no longer afford. His sleeping partner learned to breathe quietly, adjusting their own movements to avoid waking him. Elias had come to believe that the dark was not an absence of light, but a presence of unseen threat, a space where the ground could give way again without warning. His work as a salesperson soon intersected with this new landscape. He was certain that his attention had simply fractured. During morning briefings or client walkthroughs, his thoughts would scatter across floor plans and commission structures, leaving him stranded in the middle of a pitch. He would watch a prospect’s lips move while his own voice faltered, frustration mounting with every missed follow-up. The two states sat side by side in his chest: the quiet, heavy pull of guilt and shame that never fully receded, and the sharp, scattered inability to hold a single thread long enough to close a deal. Neither dictated the other; they simply occupied the same room, demanding separate portions of his energy. The potency of his world tightened on a Tuesday afternoon in a corporate lobby. Elias was walking toward a client’s office when a maintenance crew dropped a heavy steel tool cart behind a security desk. The metallic crash echoed off the glass partitions, sharp and percussive. His breath caught. The fear surged, hot and immediate, braiding itself with a wave of horror and a familiar, hollow guilt. He did not run, but he stepped back, his concentration snapping completely. He lost the thread of his sales narrative mid-sentence, his eyes darting to the service corridor, certain that another collapse was imminent. He avoided the service elevators after that, taking a longer route through the underground parking garage, a detour that now added twenty minutes to his day and made him late to his afternoon calls. The avoidance was not a strategy he had chosen; it was just the only way to keep the floor from opening up beneath him. What finally brought him to the clinic was the realization that he could no longer navigate his own office building without bracing for impact, and that his exhaustion was beginning to echo in the quiet hours with his partner. He walked into the intake room with a notebook full of missed appointments and a quiet, desperate hope that someone might help him untangle the knot in his chest. What he fears most is losing himself completely to the echo of a place he never wanted to know, hoping instead to reclaim the simple, unremarkable safety of an ordinary evening.
